claim: SETD3 knockout in HEK293T cells greatly reduced τ-N-methylhistidine.
source: Because SETD3 modifies abundant actin proteins (Dai et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Kwiatkowski et al., 2018; Wilkinson et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2020), SETD3 knockout (KO) in HEK293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E) greatly reduced τ-N-methylhistidine (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and references to prior work on SETD3's role in actin modification.

claim: A substantial fraction of τ-N-methylhistidine remained in SETD3 KO cells, suggesting the presence of other mammalian τ-N-methyltransferase(s).
source: However, a substantial fraction of τ-N-methylhistidine was left in the SETD3 KO cells (Figure 1A), suggesting the presence of other mammalian τ-N-methyltransferase(s).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from Figure 1A showing residual τ-N-methylhistidine in SETD3 KO cells, and logical inference about the existence of other enzymes.

claim: SETD3-METTL18 double-KO cells had even lower levels of τ-N-methylhistidine than SETD3 single-KO cells.
source: Indeed, the SETD3-METTL18 double-KO (DKO) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E) had even lower levels of τ-N- methylhistidine than the SETD3 single-KO cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing τ-N-methylhistidine levels in different knockout cell lines.

claim: No significant alteration in π-N-methylhistidine was detected in any cells tested in this study.
source: Note that we could not detect any significant alteration in π-N-methylhistidine in any cells tested in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Human RPL3 was the only candidate protein reproducibly identified as a METTL18 substrate in ProSeAM-SILAC experiments.
source: Among the detected proteins, human RPL3 was the only candidate to be reproducibly identified (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ProSeAM-SILAC mass spectrometry shown in Figure 1D.

claim: His245 of RPL3 is methylated in cellular RPL3.
source: This analysis identified the methylhistidine in cellular RPL3 and precisely annotated the residue at His245 (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1E identifying the methylation site.

claim: METTL18 KO cells did not show methylated His245 in RPL3.
source: In stark contrast, the same experiments with METTL18 KO did not detect methylated His245 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F comparing methylation in wild-type and METTL18 KO cells.

claim: Ectopic expression of wild-type METTL18 in KO cells rescued the His245 methylation.
source: The ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) METTL18 in the KO cells rescued the modification, whereas mutations in the potential SAM binding site (Asp193Lys-Gly195Arg-Gly197Arg), which were predicted based on lysine methyltransferase orthologs (Ng et al., 2002), abolished the potential (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and references to prior work on SAM binding sites.

claim: Mutations in the potential SAM binding site (Asp193Lys-Gly195Arg-Gly197Arg) of METTL18 abolished methylation activity.
source: The ectopic expression of wild-type (WT) METTL18 in the KO cells rescued the modification, whereas mutations in the potential SAM binding site (Asp193Lys-Gly195Arg-Gly197Arg), which were predicted based on lysine methyltransferase orthologs (Ng et al., 2002), abolished the potential (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and references to prior work on SAM binding sites.

claim: METTL18-dependent His245 methylation was found in endogenous RPL3 isolated in the 60S subunit.
source: The same METTL18-dependent His245 methylation was also found in endogenous RPL3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D), isolated in the 60S subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Methylation on His245 of RPL3 occurs at the τ-N position but not at the π-N position.
source: To distinguish the methylation forms on histidine, we applied MRM to the peptide fragments containing His245 and clearly observed that methylation occurs at the τ-N position but not at the π-N position (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by MRM mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: His245 of RPL3 is a METTL18 substrate for the formation of τ-N-methylhistidine in cells.
source: Thus, taken together, our data demonstrated that His245 of RPL3 is a METTL18 substrate for the formation of τ-N-methylhistidine in cells.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Immunopurified FLAG-tagged RPL3 proteins from METTL18 KO cells were efficiently labeled by recombinant METTL18 using 14C-labeled SAM.
source: Irrespective of the human or mouse homolog, the immunopurified FLAG-tagged RPL3 proteins transiently expressed in METTL18 KO cells were efficiently labeled by recombinant METTL18 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro methylation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Changing His245 to Ala completely abolished the methylation reaction by METTL18.
source: Moreover, changing His245 to Ala completely abolished the reaction, validating His245 as a methylation site.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the in vitro methylation assay.

claim: Recombinant RPL3 expressed in bacteria was a poor substrate for METTL18 methylation.
source: In contrast, recombinant RPL3 expressed in bacteria was a poor substrate (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro methylation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A similar deficiency in the in vitro methylation assay by Hpm1 on solo RPL3 protein produced in bacteria was seen in yeast.
source: A similar deficiency in the in vitro methylation assay by Hpm1 on solo RPL3 protein produced in bacteria was seen in yeast (Al-Hadid et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on yeast Hpm1.

claim: METTL18 recognizes RPL3 within ribosomes or preassembled intermediates.
source: Given that RPL3 expressed in mammalian cells assembled into ribosomes but RPL3 expressed in bacteria did not, we hypothesized that METTL18 recognizes RPL3 within ribosomes or preassembled intermediates.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the differential methylation efficiency of RPL3 from different sources.

claim: METTL18 was associated with a complex smaller than mature 60S.
source: To characterize the molecular complex associated with METTL18, we separated the ribosomal complexes through a sucrose density gradient and found that METTL18 was associated with a complex smaller than mature 60S (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sucrose density gradient data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The METTL18-associating complex is pre-60S in the middle of biogenesis.
source: Given the smaller size, we speculated that the METTL18-associating complex is pre-60S in the middle of biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the size of the METTL18-associated complex.

claim: The METTL18-containing subfractions possessed PES1, a ribosome biogenesis factor at an early step.
source: Indeed, the METTL18-containing subfractions also possessed PES1 (a yeast Nop7 homolog), a ribosome biogenesis factor at an early step (Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018), and a small portion of RPL3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and references to prior work on PES1.

claim: NMD3 was almost exclusive to the METTL18-associating pre-60S.
source: On the other hand, NMD3, an adaptor protein of the late-stage pre-60S for cytoplasmic export (Ma et al., 2017; Malyutin et al., 2017), was almost exclusive to the METTL18-associating pre-60S.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data and references to prior work on NMD3.

claim: RPL3 in an early intermediate complex of 60S biogenesis is an efficient substrate for METTL18.
source: These data suggested that RPL3, in an early intermediate complex of 60S biogenesis, is an efficient substrate for METTL18.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the co-fractionation data of METTL18 with early pre-60S markers.

claim: No altered abundance of the 60S subunit (relative to the 40S subunit) was observed in METTL18 KO cells.
source: However, assessed by the bulk 28S rRNA abundance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the 60S fraction in sucrose density gradient (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), no altered abundance of the 60S subunit (relative to the 40S subunit) was observed in METTL18 KO cells, while the knockdown of RPL17, which is known to hamper 60S biogenesis (Wang et al., 2015), reduced the 60S abundance in a sucrose density gradient (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rRNA abundance and sucrose gradient data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and references to prior work on RPL17.

claim: τ-N-methylated RPL3 is a stoichiometric component of the ribosome.
source: To understand the potential role of methylation in RPL3, we reanalyzed published cryo-EM data (Osterman et al., 2020) and assessed the τ-N-methyl moiety on His245 of RPL3 (Figure 3A), which indicated that τ-N-methylated RPL3 is a stoichiometric component of the ribosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 3A and references to published cryo-EM data.

claim: A similar density of methylation on the histidine of RPL3 has been found in rabbit ribosomes.
source: A similar density of methylation on the histidine of RPL3 has also been found in rabbit ribosomes (Bhatt et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on rabbit ribosomes.

claim: Ribosomes isolated from METTL18 KO cells lost density at the τ-N position of His245.
source: On the other hand, the ribosomes isolated from METTL18 KO cells lost density at the τ-N position of the His245 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absence of methylation at the τ-N position allowed nitrogen to form hydrogen bonds with G1595 of 28S rRNA.
source: The absence of methylation at the τ-N position allowed nitrogen to form hydrogen bonds with G1595 of 28S rRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: G1595 is located in the loop of helix 35, which macrolide antibiotics target in bacterial systems.
source: Given that G1595 is located in the loop of helix 35, which macrolide antibiotics target in bacterial systems (Kannan and Mankin, 2011), this difference in the interaction between His245 and G1595 suggests an alteration in the translation reaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on macrolide antibiotic targets and inference about translation effects.

claim: No significant difference in overall translation was detected in METTL18 KO cells as probed by polysome formation.
source: However, we could not detect a significant difference in overall translation probed by polysome formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), whereas RPL17 knockdown reduced the polysome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant alteration in nascent peptides labeled with OP-puro was observed in METTL18 KO cells.
source: Similarly, we could not observe a significant alteration in nascent peptides labeled with O-propargyl-puromycin (OP-puro) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by OP-puro labeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Increased translation elongation of Tyr codons was found in METTL18 KO cells.
source: Strikingly, we found increased translation elongation of Tyr codons in METTL18 KO cells; ribosome occupancy on Tyr codons at the A-site was selectively reduced in the mutant cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The trend in ribosome occupancy on Tyr codons was not observed at the P and E sites.
source: This trend in ribosome occupancy was not observed at the P and E sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Tyr at the A-site was the predominant determinant for fast elongation in METTL18 KO cells.
source: Remarkably, Tyr at the A-site was the predominant determinant for fast elongation in METTL18 KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: tRNATyrGUA was noticeably reduced by METTL18 depletion.
source: However, tRNATyrGUA, which decodes both UAU and UAC codons, was noticeably reduced by METTL18 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The abundance of tRNALeuHAG was not altered by METTL18 depletion.
source: On the other hand, the abundance control tRNALeuHAG was not altered (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: tRNA abundance did not explain the reduced footprints on Tyr codons in METTL18 KO cells.
source: Thus, tRNA abundance did not explain the reduced footprints on Tyr codons.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the tRNA abundance data showing reduced tRNATyrGUA but increased elongation.

claim: The reduced footprints on Tyr codons in METTL18 KO cells were more prominent in long footprints than short footprints.
source: The reduced footprints on Tyr codons in METTL18 KO cells were more prominent in long footprints than short footprints (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Long footprints on Tyr codons were recovered by ectopic expression of METTL18 protein.
source: Moreover, the long footprints were recovered by ectopic expression of METTL18 protein (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The process or processes downstream of codon decoding are promoted in METTL18 KO cells.
source: These data suggested that the process or processes downstream of codon decoding are promoted in KO cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the long footprint data.

claim: Reduction of ribosome occupancies on Tyr codons was observed in three independent METTL18 KO HAP1 cell lines.
source: We investigated ribosome footprints on the Tyr codons in three independent METTL18 KO cell lines (1-nt, 2-nt, and 4-nt deletions) that should lead to truncated proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) and observed the reduction of ribosome occupancies on the codons in those cell lines as well (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data in HAP1 cells shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The effects of RPL3 methylation on elongation are consistent irrespective of cell type.
source: These data suggested consistent effects of RPL3 methylation on elongation irrespective of cell type.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on ribosome profiling data from both HEK293T and HAP1 cells.

claim: RPL3 methylation-deficient ribosomes exhibited faster elongation on Tyr repeats than ribosomes from naïve cells in vitro.
source: We observed that RPL3 methylation-deficient ribosomes exhibited faster elongation on Tyr repeats than ones from naïve cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RPL3 methylation mediates a slowing of translation elongation on Tyr codons.
source: These in cell and in vitro data together indicated that RPL3 methylation mediated a slowing of translation elongation on the Tyr codons.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on both ribosome profiling and in vitro translation data.

claim: Slowdown of ribosome elongation allows the duration of nascent protein folding before completion of protein synthesis.
source: Slowdown of ribosome elongation is advantageous since it allows the duration of nascent protein folding before completion of protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between elongation rate and protein folding.

claim: Translation elongation slowdown at Tyr codons by RPL3 methylation facilitates protein folding on ribosomes and maintains proper homeostasis of the proteome.
source: Therefore, we reasoned that translation elongation slowdown at Tyr codons by RPL3 methylation facilitates protein folding on ribosomes and maintains proper homeostasis of the proteome.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed effects of RPL3 methylation on elongation and established knowledge about protein folding.

claim: METTL18 depletion induced the aggregation of FlucDM but not Fluc WT reporter.
source: Indeed, METTL18 depletion induced the aggregation of FlucDM but not Fluc WT reporter (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: FlucDM protein was synthesized in METTL18 KO cells of low quality and subjected to degradation.
source: As shown by the recovery of protein abundance by treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 6C), FlucDM protein was synthesized in METTL18 KO cells of low quality and subjected to degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C showing protein recovery with proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: A subset of proteins were enriched in precipitates of METTL18 KO cell lysates.
source: We observed that a subset of proteins were enriched in precipitates of METTL18 KO cell lysates (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC-MS data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Tyr-rich proteins significantly accumulated in the precipitate subgroup from METTL18 KO cells.
source: This subgroup significantly accumulated Tyr-rich proteins (defined as proteins possessing 30 Tyr or more) (hypergeometric test, p=0.0068) (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC-MS data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The high probability of protein precipitates could not be explained by increased net protein synthesis measured by ribosome profiling.
source: The high probability of protein precipitates could not be explained by the increased net protein synthesis measured by ribosome profiling (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of SILAC and ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tyr-rich proteins were more prone to precipitate upon the deletion of METTL18 than proteins rich in other amino acids.
source: More generally, Tyr-rich proteins were more prone to precipitate upon the deletion of METTL18 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) than proteins rich in other amino acids (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC-MS data analysis shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The modulation of Tyr-specific translation elongation by RPL3 methylation confers proteome integrity.
source: Thus, proteomic analysis of cellular precipitates revealed that the modulation of Tyr-specific translation elongation by RPL3 methylation confers proteome integrity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the proteomic analysis of precipitated proteins.

claim: Metagene analysis showed prominent enrichment of TANGO-predicted aggregation propensity around Tyr codons in precipitated proteins.
source: Strikingly, metagene analysis showed prominent enrichment of the TANGO-predicted aggregation propensity around the Tyr codons (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis using TANGO shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A subset of proteins were more efficiently degraded in METTL18 KO cells as revealed by SILAC analysis with MG132 treatment.
source: Indeed, this approach revealed a subset of more efficiently degraded proteins in METTL18 KO cells (Figure 8B); this group of proteins tended to be reduced in METTL18 KO cells and recovered by MG132 treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC-MS data with proteasome inhibitor treatment shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The subset of proteins more efficiently degraded in METTL18 KO cells included Tyr-rich proteins.
source: Moreover, this subset of proteins included Tyr-rich proteins (Figure 8C), which was congruent with the enhanced elongation observed in ribosome profiling.
evidence: The claim is supported by SILAC-MS data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tyr translation modulated by RPL3-methylated ribosomes is associated with the quality of the synthesized proteins, preventing unwanted protein aggregation.
source: The relationships among the aggregation-prone character of the protein, the cellular protein precipitates, increased proteasomal substrates, and reduced ribosome occupancy indicates that Tyr translation modulated by RPL3-methylated ribosomes is associated with the quality of the synthesized proteins, preventing unwanted protein aggregation (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including aggregation, precipitation, and degradation data.

claim: METTL18 adds a methyl moiety at the τ-N position of His245 in RPL3 in the form of an early 60S biogenesis intermediate.
source: METTL18 adds a methyl moiety at the τ-N position of His245 in RPL3 in the form of an early 60S biogenesis intermediate.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Methylated ribosomes slow elongation at Tyr codons and extend the duration of nascent peptide folding, ensuring proteostatic integrity.
source: Methylated ribosomes slow elongation at Tyr codons and extend the duration of nascent peptide folding, ensuring proteostatic integrity.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Without RPL3 methylation, the accumulation of unfolded and ultimately aggregated proteins in cells was induced.
source: Without RPL3 methylation, the accumulation of unfolded and ultimately aggregated proteins in cells was induced.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human METTL18 is a histidine methyltransferase for the ribosomal protein RPL3.
source: Here, we report that human METTL18 is a histidine methyltransferase for the ribosomal protein RPL3 and that the modification specifically slows ribosome traversal on Tyr codons, allowing the proper folding of synthesized proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: RPL3 methylation specifically slows ribosome traversal on Tyr codons, allowing the proper folding of synthesized proteins.
source: Here, we report that human METTL18 is a histidine methyltransferase for the ribosomal protein RPL3 and that the modification specifically slows ribosome traversal on Tyr codons, allowing the proper folding of synthesized proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: His245 of RPL3 is methylated at the τ-N position by METTL18.
source: By performing an in vitro methylation assay with a methyl donor analog and quantitative mass spectrometry, we found that His245 of RPL3 is methylated at the τ-N position by METTL18.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Structural comparison of the modified and unmodified ribosomes showed stoichiometric modification.
source: Structural comparison of the modified and unmodified ribosomes showed stoichiometric modification and suggested a role in translation reactions.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Genome-wide ribosome profiling and an in vitro translation assay revealed that translation elongation at Tyr codons was suppressed by RPL3 methylation.
source: Indeed, genome-wide ribosome profiling and an in vitro translation assay revealed that translation elongation at Tyr codons was suppressed by RPL3 methylation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Slower elongation provides enough time for nascent protein folding.
source: Because the slower elongation provides enough time for nascent protein folding, RPL3 methylation protects cells from the cellular aggregation of Tyr-rich proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: RPL3 methylation protects cells from the cellular aggregation of Tyr-rich proteins.
source: Because the slower elongation provides enough time for nascent protein folding, RPL3 methylation protects cells from the cellular aggregation of Tyr-rich proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Histidine methylation is an example of a ribosome modification that ensures proteome integrity in cells.
source: Our results reveal histidine methylation as an example of a ribosome modification that ensures proteome integrity in cells.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Protein methylation occurs predominantly on lysine and arginine residues, but histidine also serves as a methylation substrate.
source: Protein methylation occurs predominantly on lysine and arginine residues, but histidine also serves as a methylation substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about protein methylation.

claim: A limited number of enzymes responsible for histidine methylation have been reported.
source: However, a limited number of enzymes responsible for this modification have been reported.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of the field at the time of the study.

claim: The biological role of histidine methylation has remained poorly understood.
source: Moreover, the biological role of histidine methylation has remained poorly understood to date.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of the field at the time of the study.

claim: Protein methylation influences the function of proteins and provides a convertible platform for the modulation of cellular processes.
source: This modification influences the function of proteins and provides a convertible platform for the modulation of cellular processes, including interactions with other molecules, protein structure, localization, and enzymatic activity (Biggar and Li, 2015; Clarke, 2018; Murn and Shi, 2017; Rodríguez-Paredes and Lyko, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The majority of protein methylation has been observed on lysine and arginine amino acids.
source: Whereas the majority of protein methylation has been observed on lysine and arginine amino acids (Biggar and Li, 2015; Clarke, 2018; Murn and Shi, 2017; Rodríguez-Paredes and Lyko, 2019), histidine residues also supply alternative target sites for methylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Histidine methylation was previously thought to be restricted to limited proteins.
source: Although this modification was previously thought to be restricted to limited proteins (Webb et al., 2010), a recent comprehensive survey suggested widespread occurrence in the proteome (Davydova et al., 2021; Ning et al., 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on prior scientific understanding supported by citation.

claim: A recent comprehensive survey suggested widespread occurrence of histidine methylation in the proteome.
source: Although this modification was previously thought to be restricted to limited proteins (Webb et al., 2010), a recent comprehensive survey suggested widespread occurrence in the proteome (Davydova et al., 2021; Ning et al., 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on recent scientific findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two distinct nitrogen atoms in histidine could be methylated: the π-N position and the τ-N position.
source: Two distinct nitrogen atoms in histidine could be methylated: the π-N position (π-N-methylhistidine or 1-methylhistidine) and the τ-N position (τ-N-methylhistidine or 3-methylhistidine) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on established chemical knowledge about histidine structure.

claim: METTL9 and SETD3 are the only known mammalian protein methyltransferases for π-N-methylhistidine and τ-N-methylhistidine, respectively.
source: Regarding their responsible enzymes, methyltransferase-like (METTL) 9 – a seven β-strand methyltransferase – and SET domain containing 3 (SETD3) are, as of yet, the only known mammalian protein methyltransferases for π-N-methylhistidine (Davydova et al., 2021) and τ-N-methylhistidine (Dai et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Kwiatkowski et al., 2018; Wilkinson et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2020), respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of the field at the time of the study, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The landscape of histidine methyltransferase-substrate pairs and the physiological functions of the modification have remained largely elusive.
source: Nevertheless, the landscape of histidine methyltransferase-substrate pairs and, more importantly, the physiological functions of the modification have remained largely elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of the field at the time of the study.

claim: The ribosome is a hotspot for PTM.
source: Recent emerging studies have shown that the ribosome is a hotspot for PTM (Emmott et al., 2019; Simsek and Barna, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on recent scientific findings supported by citations.

claim: PTMs on ribosomal proteins may regulate protein synthesis in specific contexts.
source: Indeed, PTMs on ribosomal proteins may regulate protein synthesis in specific contexts, such as a subset of transcripts (Imami et al., 2018; Kapasi et al., 2007; Mazumder et al., 2003), the cell cycle (Imami et al., 2018), stress response (Higgins et al., 2015; Matsuki et al., 2020), and differentiation (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on scientific findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: Yeast homolog of METTL18 (Hpm1) catalyzes τ-N-methylation on histidine in Rpl3.
source: An apparent candidate for the remaining τ-N-methyltransferase in SETD3 KO cells was METTL18, whose yeast homolog (histidine protein methyltransferase 1 [Hpm1]) has been reported to catalyze τ-N-methylation on histidine in Rpl3 (Al-Hadid et al., 2016; Al-Hadid et al., 2014; Webb et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work in yeast supported by multiple citations.

claim: τ-N-methylation at His243 in yeast Rpl3 has been indirectly demonstrated.
source: Whereas τ-N-methylation at the equivalent residue (His243) in yeast Rpl3 has been indirectly demonstrated (Webb et al., 2010), this study provided solid evidence (such as MS and cryo-EM) of the modification on the homolog in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work in yeast supported by citation.

claim: Human RPL3 alone could not be methylated by METTL18, similar to prior yeast work.
source: Similar to prior yeast work (Al-Hadid et al., 2014), human RPL3 alone could not be methylated by METTL18.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data in this study and comparison to prior yeast work.

claim: His245 of RPL3 in the early pre-60S in state B is exposed to solvent, possibly enabling access to METTL18.
source: In the recent structural studies on pre-60 assembly intermediates (Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018), His245 of RPL3 in the early pre-60S in state B (Kater et al., 2017) is exposed to solvent (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A), possibly enabling access to METTL18, although His245 per se was not visible in the structure because of flexibility.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of published structural data supported by citations.

claim: Ribosomal proteins and rRNAs in the later stage of 60S biogenesis (at state D) fill the space corresponding to His245.
source: In contrast, ribosomal proteins and rRNAs in the later stage of 60S biogenesis (at state D) (Kater et al., 2017) fill the corresponding space (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of published structural data supported by citation.

claim: Histidine methylation by METTL18 should be restricted to specific timing of the macromolecule assembly.
source: Thus, histidine methylation by METTL18 should be restricted to specific timing of the macromolecule assembly.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural analysis of pre-60S intermediates.

claim: A paper from Falnes and coworkers reached a similar conclusion regarding the methylation site (His245 in RPL3) and the methylation type (τ-N position) mediated by human METTL18.
source: In the course of this work, a paper from Falnes and coworkers was published and reached a similar conclusion regarding the methylation site (His245 in RPL3) and the methylation type (τ-N position) mediated by human METTL18 (Małecki et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: Recombinant METTL18 protein methylated isolated ribosomes from METTL18 KO, as shown in an earlier report.
source: Although the earlier report showed that recombinant METTL18 protein methylated isolated ribosomes from METTL18 KO, the authors also observed that METTL18 localized in nucleoli (Małecki et al., 2021) where ribosomes are still under assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: The purified ribosome may consist of contaminated pre-60S, and this fraction was an efficient substrate of METTL18.
source: These data could be interpreted to show that the purified ribosome may consist of contaminated pre-60S, and this fraction was an efficient substrate of METTL18.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of data from a concurrent publication.

claim: An earlier report showed that ribosome profiling in METTL18 KO HAP1 cells revealed widespread effects of translation elongation, exemplified by slowdown of the GAA codon.
source: In the earlier report, ribosome profiling in METTL18 KO HAP1 cells revealed widespread effects of translation elongation, exemplified by slowdown of the GAA codon (Małecki et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a concurrent publication.

claim: METTL18 KO enhanced ribosome traversal on Tyr codons in HEK293T and HAP1 cells in this study.
source: In contrast, the same experiment in this work with HEK293T and HAP1 (including the same cell line [2-nt del.] used in Małecki et al., 2021) showed that METTL18 KO enhanced ribosome traversal on Tyr codons (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from this study.

claim: The effect of RPL3 methylation on translation elongation could be dynamic and dependent on cellular status affected by circumstances.
source: The effect of RPL3 methylation on translation elongation could be dynamic and dependent on cellular status affected by circumstances (e.g., culturing conditions).
evidence: The claim is speculation about the context-dependent effects of RPL3 methylation.

claim: The modification-mediated ribosome slowdown provides a unique example of translational control since modification in general often offers a smooth translation, as exemplified in tRNA modifications.
source: The modification-mediated ribosome slowdown revealed in this study provides a unique example of translational control since modification in general often offers a smooth translation, as exemplified in tRNA modifications (Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Tuorto et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to established knowledge about tRNA modifications supported by citations.

claim: The exact mechanism of how His245 methylation in RPL3 leads to Tyr-specific elongation retardation remains elusive.
source: The exact mechanism of how His245 methylation in RPL3 leads to Tyr-specific elongation retardation remains elusive.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: In bacteria, the loop of helix 35 was heavily modified, although the role of rRNA modification has been unclear.
source: In bacteria, the loop of helix 35, where unmethylated His245 interacts, was heavily modified (Kannan and Mankin, 2011), although the role of rRNA modification has been unclear.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work in bacteria supported by citation.

claim: Eukaryotic RPL3 may functionally replace RNA modification by histidine methylation.
source: Eukaryotic RPL3 may functionally replace RNA modification by histidine methylation.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on comparison to bacterial systems.

claim: His245 is located in the 'basic thumb' region (Arg234-Arg246), which bridges the interaction of 28S rRNA helices and facilitates the formation of an aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor.
source: From another viewpoint, His245 is located in the 'basic thumb' region (Arg234-Arg246), which bridges the interaction of 28S rRNA helices (H61, H73, and H90) and facilitates the formation of a so-called 'aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor' (Meskauskas and Dinman, 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on prior structural and functional work supported by citation.

claim: The methylation of His245 may allosterically alter the dynamic character of the aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor to restrict the movement of charged Tyr on tRNA.
source: Thus, the methylation of His245 may allosterically alter the dynamic character of the aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor to restrict the movement of charged Tyr on tRNA.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the mechanism of RPL3 methylation effects.

claim: Conformational changes in the aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor were suggested by molecular dynamics simulation.
source: Indeed, conformational changes in the aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation corridor were suggested by molecular dynamics simulation (Gulay et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on prior computational work supported by citation.

claim: An earlier report in yeast suggested that Hpm1 deletion decreased the fidelity of translation, inducing stop codon readthrough.
source: Indeed, an earlier report in yeast suggested that Hpm1 (a homolog of METTL18) deletion decreased the fidelity of translation, inducing stop codon readthrough (Al-Hadid et al., 2016; Al-Hadid et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work in yeast supported by citations.

claim: Ribosome profiling data in HEK293T cells did not show any increase in ribosome footprints in the 3′ UTR that could be accumulated by stop codon readthrough.
source: However, our ribosome profiling data in HEK293T cells did not show any increase in ribosome footprints in the 3′ UTR (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C and D) that could be accumulated by the stop codon readthrough (Arribere et al., 2016; Dunn et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from this study and references to prior work on stop codon readthrough.

claim: Ribosome traversal along the CDS is generally defined by the decoding rate in bacteria and yeasts.
source: Although ribosome traversal along the CDS is generally defined by the decoding rate in bacteria (Mohammad et al., 2019) and yeasts (Hussmann et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019), the codon/amino acid-specific effects of RPL3 histidine methylation in humans suggest that the landscape is more complex in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome dynamics in bacteria and yeast supported by citations.

claim: Ribosome occupancy in mammals is poorly predicted by tRNA abundance in cells.
source: Indeed, ribosome occupancy in mammals is poorly predicted by tRNA abundance in cells (Han et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work in mammals supported by citation.

claim: A wide array of ribosome modifications, including RPL3 histidine modification, ultimately define the speed of ribosome movement and thus the quality of protein synthesized in cells.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that a wide array of ribosome modifications, including RPL3 histidine modification, ultimately define the speed of ribosome movement and thus the quality of protein synthesized in cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the findings of this study and broader context of ribosome modifications.

claim: SETD3 modifies abundant actin proteins.
source: Because SETD3 modifies abundant actin proteins (Dai et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2019; Kwiatkowski et al., 2018; Wilkinson et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2020), SETD3 knockout (KO) in HEK293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E) greatly reduced τ-N-methylhistidine (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work on SETD3 supported by multiple citations.

claim: ProSeAM acts as a donor in the methylation reaction by the SET domain and 7-β-strand methyltransferase.
source: For this purpose, we harnessed propargylic Se-adenosyl-l-selenomethionine (ProSeAM), an analog of S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM). This compound acts as a donor in the methylation reaction by the SET domain and 7-β-strand methyltransferase (Davydova et al., 2021; Shimazu et al., 2014; Shimazu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work on ProSeAM supported by multiple citations.

claim: RPL17 knockdown is known to hamper 60S biogenesis.
source: However, assessed by the bulk 28S rRNA abundance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the 60S fraction in sucrose density gradient (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), no altered abundance of the 60S subunit (relative to the 40S subunit) was observed in METTL18 KO cells, while the knockdown of RPL17, which is known to hamper 60S biogenesis (Wang et al., 2015), reduced the 60S abundance in a sucrose density gradient (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is based on prior work on RPL17 supported by citation.

claim: Ribosome footprints possess two distinct populations of different lengths (short, peaked at ~22 nt; long, peaked at ~29 nt), reflecting the presence of A-site tRNA.
source: Ribosome footprints possess two distinct populations of different lengths (short, peaked at ~22 nt; long, peaked at ~29 nt), reflecting the presence of A-site tRNA (Lareau et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome footprint populations supported by citations.

claim: Short footprints represent nonrotated ribosomes waiting for A-site codon decoding by tRNA.
source: Since A-site tRNA-free ribosomes are more susceptible to RNase treatment at the 3′ end, the trimmed short footprints represent nonrotated ribosomes waiting for A-site codon decoding by tRNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome footprint interpretation.

claim: Long footprints originate from ribosomes accommodated with A-site tRNA in the middle of the peptidyl transfer reaction or subsequent subunit rotation.
source: On the other hand, long footprints originate from ribosomes accommodated with A-site tRNA in the middle of the peptidyl transfer reaction or subsequent subunit rotation (Lareau et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome footprint interpretation supported by citations.
